summary:
Genesis opens the Bible with the line that supplies its Hebrew title: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth" (1:1) — Bereshit, "in the beginning"; the English title, from the book's Greek translation, means "origin." The book moves in two unequal parts: chapters 1–11 cover the whole world (creation, Eden, the flood, Babel), and chapters 12–50 follow a single family for four generations, from Abraham to Joseph. A recurring heading marks the seams: "This is the account of..." (Hebrew toledot, "generations") introduces each section, from "the account of the heavens and the earth" (2:4) to "the account of Jacob" (37:2).

Creation unfolds in six days of work and a seventh of rest, with humanity made "in His own image," "male and female" (1:27). Readers divide over the days — ordinary days, long ages, or a literary framework — and the text does not settle it. Adam and Eve eat from the forbidden tree and are exiled from Eden, though the sentence on the serpent, "He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel" (3:15), has long been read as the Bible's first pointer to a coming deliverer. Cain murders Abel; the earth becomes "full of violence" (6:11) and is drowned in the flood, with Noah's family preserved in the ark; and at Babel a united humanity builds a tower "that we may make a name for ourselves" (11:4) and is scattered into many languages.

At chapter 12 the story narrows to one household. Abram — seventy-five, childless, his family migrated from Ur of the Chaldeans in Mesopotamia to Haran — is told, "Leave your country, your kindred, and your father's household, and go to the land I will show you," with a promise: "all the families of the earth will be blessed through you" (12:1–3). God then seals the promise as a covenant, a formal oath-bound pact: in chapter 15 a smoking firepot and flaming torch pass between halved animal carcasses, an ancient treaty rite, and in chapter 17 circumcision becomes its sign and the couple receive new names, Abraham and Sarah. "Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness" (15:6) becomes a foundation text for Paul (Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6). Isaac is born when Abraham is a hundred, and chapter 22 tests everything: God commands Abraham to offer "your only son Isaac, whom you love" on Mount Moriah, and stops him only as the knife is raised.

Isaac's twin sons split the family. Jacob buys Esau's birthright for a meal of stew, takes the firstborn's blessing by disguise, and flees to his uncle Laban for twenty years, where he is tricked in turn: he gets Leah in place of Rachel on his wedding night. On the road home a stranger wrestles him until daybreak and renames him: "Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed" (32:28). His twelve sons become Israel's twelve tribes, and the last fourteen chapters follow one of them. Joseph — the favorite, sold into Egypt by his brothers, falsely imprisoned, then raised up to manage Egypt's grain after interpreting Pharaoh's dreams of famine — saves the family that sold him. His verdict on it all: "As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good ... to preserve the lives of many people" (50:20).

The book does not end in the promised land. Jacob's household, "seventy in all" (46:27), settles in Goshen in Egypt, matching what God had told Abram: "your descendants will be strangers in a land that is not their own, and they will be enslaved and mistreated four hundred years" (15:13). Joseph makes the sons of Israel swear to "carry my bones up from this place" when God brings them back (50:25), an oath kept at the exodus (Exodus 13:19). The book's last words leave that pledge waiting: Joseph embalmed and laid "in a coffin in Egypt" (50:26).
